# Introduction

## Outline

* P1: Immunomodulatory receptors are key therapeutic targets but generate limiting off-target effects.
    + Molecules that interact with surface receptors are the largest class of therapeutics.
    + Immunomodulatory receptors often dictate immune cell function and are thus involved in a broad range of immune-mediated diseases.
    + Two properties of immune receptors:
        * Shared receptor expression across cells of different functions leads to off-target binding
        * Cellular pleiotropy leads to counteractive signals in off-target cells
    + Combined, these features lead to off-target binding which produces signals that counteract the desired effect (at best) and generate severe adverse effects (at worst)
    + Immunomodulatory ligands are rarely adopted because of severe adverse effects that arise from off-target binding.
* P2: Protein engineering efforts have reduced off-target binding through avidity-dependent targeting.
    + The promise of immunomodulatory molecules has spurred extensive protein engineering efforts aimed at reducing off-target binding
    + Chief among these are multivalent, affinity-engineered cytokine muteins fused to targeted antibody scaffolds (targeted, multispecific cytokine fusions) 
    + Coordinated changes in affinity and valency allow these molecules to preferentially bind target cells despite modest differences in receptor expression between target and off-target populations.
    + These molecules owe this so-called cell-type selectivity to avidity effects wherein low-affinity, multivalent molecules require high receptor density to bind effectively
* P3: Often, binding is all that matters.
    + Multispecific molecules with decoupled signaling and targeting domains have been shown to further enhance cell-type selectivity
    + In these cases, high-affinity and/or high-valency targeting subunits direct signal domain binding toward target cells, while low-affinity signal domains are unable to bind off-target cells despite high signal receptor density
    + Similarly, antibody-drug conjugates use targeting domains to direct cytotoxic payloads based on surface protein expression
    + Considering only the targeting function of surface proteins reveals a vast number of potential surface targets which might be exploited alone or in combination.
* P4: Combinatorial complexity has left the development of multispecific, targeted therapeutics unguided.
    + Evolution has granted us with thousands of unique surface proteins
    + These proteins may, in some combination, facilitate perfectly selective delivery of signal to any given cell type
    + However, the number of possible combinations of surface proteins is combinatorially large
    + This complexity has left the field of multispecificity unguided and siloed.
    + Even systematic explorations neglect to comprehensively evaluate the selectivity of the large space of possible targets, especially across different target cell types
* P5: Here, we use a high-throughput computational platform to systematically explore the multi-receptor targeting space and identify key properties of multispecificity.

## Body

The ubiquitous involvement of immune r

Immunomodulatory receptors are key therapeutic targets for broad range of diseases. The largest class of immune receptors are cell-surface proteins that bind secreted signaling proteins to elicit potent cellular responses, such as ___. The breadth and diversity of ligand--receptor pairs has armed the immune system with the ability to sense and respond to a nearly endless array of environmental cues. Conversely, dysregulation of ligand–-receptor interactions leads to a number of diseases, including ___. Harnessing the immunomodulatory capabilities of these receptors constitutes a major step toward attaining full control over immune functions.

Attempts to control immune function by administering immunomodulatory proteins have broadly resulted in dose-limiting toxicities. Immune receptors exhibit two unique properties that hinder these efforts. First, immune receptors are seldom solely expressed on cells of a single function---distinct cell types often express similar amounts and kinds of immune receptors. Second, the signal generated upon binding these receptors is heavily influenced by cellular context. In combination, these properties expose the observed limitation: upon administration, a protein binds its cognate receptor on both target and off-target cells, followed by the induction of distinct, often counterproductive, responses from each cell type. The key challenge in targeting immune receptors is therefore engineering ligands that preferentially bind target cells over off-target populations.

Two arms of protein engineering methods have improved the safety and efficacy of immunomodulatory proteins by driving binding toward target cells. First, amino-acid sequence mutations have achieved receptor-subunit--level affinity tuning, biasing binding toward target cells based on differences in subunit expression levels. Second, multivalent ligand complexes have improved selectivity by exploiting increases in local concentration upon binding. Through these so-called avidity effects, multivalent molecules exhibit increased sensitivity to differences in receptor density between populations of cells. Coordinated changes in affinity and valency have produced molecules that preferentially bind target cells despite only modest differences in receptor expression between target and off-target populations.

Multispecific ligand complexes build upon affinity and valency engineering strategies by decoupling signaling from targeting. Such molecules generally drive binding toward target cells through high-affinity "targeting" subunits, whose cognate receptors are uniquely expressed on target cells. Once bound, these molecules exert their effects locally either through avidity-driven binding of low-affinity "signaling" subunits, or through local exposure/release of cytotoxic payloads. In either case, target receptor binding is the key determinant of cell-type selectivity. Optimizing multispecific ligand design for target cell binding unlocks a vast number of potential surface targets, which, when targeted in some combination, might enable uniquely selective delivery to a given cell type.

The design process of multispecific proteins is critically bottlenecked by the combinatorial complexity of possible target combinations. Here, we aim to systematically explore the multi-receptor targeting space to identify key properties of multispecificity.
